items.title: Section: Six Reasons Not to Ordain Someone — And the Crucial Difference Between a Fraud and a Changed Heart

items.zh: 問：由幾因緣，雖樂欲受苾芻律儀，而不應授？答：苾芻律儀略由六因。一、意樂損害，二、依止損害，三、男形損害，四、白法損害，五、繫屬於他，六、為護他故。若有為王之所逼錄，或為強賊之所逼錄，或為債主之所逼迫，或由怖畏之所逼迫，或畏不活。彼如是思：我處居家，難可存活，是諸苾芻活命甚易。我今應往苾芻眾中，詐現自身與彼同法，易當活命。彼由如是諂詐意樂，既出家已，雖懷恐怖，守護奉行隨一學處，勿諸苾芻與我同止，知我犯戒，便當驅擯。然彼意樂被損害故，不名出家受具足戒，如是名為意樂損害。若復有人作如是思：我處居家，難可活命，要當出家方易存濟。如諸苾芻所修梵行，我亦如是，乃至命終當修梵行。如是出家者，不名意樂損害。雖非純淨，非不說名出家受具。
items.en:
First, presenting who should not be ordained; first, subsumed under monastic restraint; first, the question. Question: for how many reasons, though a person wishes to receive monastic restraint, should ordination not be given?
Second, the answer; first, six reasons; first, stating and listing. Answer: monastic restraint is withheld, in brief, for six reasons: first, damaged motivation; second, damaged physical basis; third, damaged male form; fourth, damaged wholesome capacity; fifth, being subject to another's authority; sixth, the need to protect others' confidence.
First, damaged motivation; first, presenting its varieties. If someone is driven by a king's persecution, a powerful bandit's pursuit, a creditor's demands, overwhelming fear, or the dread of being unable to survive.
Second, distinguishing the appropriate cases; first, genuine damage; first, presenting their reasoning. Such a person thinks: living at home, I can hardly survive, while these monastics live with such ease — I shall go among the monastic assembly and falsely present myself as one of their own, so as to survive more easily.
Second, clarifying the damage. Having ordained with this deceitful, false motivation, though harbouring fear, this person still guards and upholds some of the training precepts, thinking: may the monastics dwelling with me never discover my violation and expel me. Yet because their motivation is damaged in this way, they are not called one who has left household life and received full ordination — this is called damaged motivation.
Second, no genuine damage; first, presenting their reasoning. But if someone instead thinks: living at home, I can hardly survive, and I should indeed leave household life to make my life sustainable — moreover, I too shall practice the very pure conduct these monastics practice, for as long as I live.
Second, clarifying there is no damage. Such a person who leaves household life is not said to have damaged motivation. Though their beginning was not pure, they are not thereby excluded from being called one who has left household life and received full ordination.

items.title: Section: Serious Illness as a Bar to Ordination — Why Even Sincere Devotion Cannot Overcome an Unsustainable Burden

items.zh: 若有身帶癰腫等疾，如遮法中所說病狀，如是名為依止損害。由彼依止被損害故，雖復出家，然無力能供事師長。彼由如是無力能故，所受師長、同梵行者供事之業，及受純信施主衣服、飲食等淨信施物，此之二種淨信所施彼極難消，不應受用，令彼退減諸善法故。
items.en:
Second, damaged physical basis; first, presenting this category. Whoever carries serious afflictions such as festering sores or growths, matching the conditions described among the traditional obstacles, is said to have damaged physical basis.
Second, explaining the reason. Because their physical basis is damaged, even having left household life, they are unable to serve their own teachers. Lacking this capacity, they instead require service from their teachers and fellow practitioners, while also receiving devoted donors' offerings of clothing, food, and other necessities — both kinds of devoted offering become extremely difficult for them to properly receive, and accepting them regardless causes their own wholesome qualities to diminish.

items.title: Section: Three Kinds of Damaged Male Form — Absent from Birth, Intermittent, and Injured

items.zh: 是故依止被損害者，不應出家受具足戒。若扇搋迦及半擇迦，名男形損害，不應出家受具足戒。當知因緣如前已說。又半擇迦略有三種。一、全分半擇迦，二、一分半擇迦，三、損害半擇迦。若有生便不成男根，是名全分半擇迦。若有半月起男勢用；或有被他於己為過，或復見他行非梵行，男勢方起；是名一分半擇迦。若被刀等之所損害，或為病藥、若火呪等之所損害，先得男根今被斷壞，既斷壞已，男勢不轉。是名損害半擇迦。初半擇迦名半擇迦，亦扇搋迦。第二唯半擇迦，非扇搋迦。第三若不被他於己為過，唯扇搋迦，非半擇迦；若有被他於己為過，名半擇迦，亦扇搋迦。
items.en:
Third, concluding this bars ordination. Therefore, one whose physical basis is damaged should not leave household life or receive full ordination.
Third, damaged male form; first, briefly; first, stating it. The ṣaṇḍhaka and the paṇḍaka are said to have damaged male form, and should not leave household life or receive full ordination. Second, referring back. One should know the reasoning is as already explained before.
Second, in full detail; first, stating and listing. The paṇḍaka is, in brief, of three kinds: first, complete; second, partial; third, damaged.
Second, explaining each; first, the complete kind. Whoever lacks male capacity entirely from birth is the complete kind.
Second, the partial kind. Whoever has male capacity arising only for half of each month, or only upon being mocked by another, or only upon witnessing another's sexual conduct, is the partial kind.
Third, the damaged kind. Whoever once possessed male capacity, now destroyed through injury by a blade, by illness or medication, by fire, or by sorcery, so that capacity no longer functions, is the damaged kind.
Third, a careful analysis. The first kind is called paṇḍaka and also ṣaṇḍhaka. The second is called only paṇḍaka, not ṣaṇḍhaka. The third, if not also subject to others' mockery, is called only ṣaṇḍhaka, not paṇḍaka; if also subject to mockery, it is called paṇḍaka and also ṣaṇḍhaka.

items.title: Section: Damaged Wholesome Capacity — When Past Conduct Has Already Undermined the Very Shame That Precepts Depend On

items.zh: 若造無間業，污苾芻尼，外道賊住，若別異住，若不共住，是名白法損害。不應為授具足戒。所以者何？彼由上品無慚無愧極垢染法，令慚愧等所有白法極成劣薄。
items.en:
Fourth, damaged wholesome capacity; first, stating this category. Whoever has committed a deed of immediate retribution, violated a nun, infiltrated as a false monastic loyal to another teaching, or is currently under disciplinary separation or expelled for a grave violation, is said to have damaged wholesome capacity, and should not be given full ordination.
Second, explaining the reason. Why is this so? Because such deeds arise from an extremely powerful absence of shame and conscience, an extremely defiling condition, causing whatever shame, conscience, and wholesome qualities remain to become extremely weakened and diminished.

items.title: Section: Nine Kinds of Not Being Free to Choose — From the King's Minister to the Child Never Told Their Own Origin

items.zh: 若諸王臣，若王所惡，若有造作王不宜業，若被債主之所拘執，若他僕隸，若他劫引，若他所得，若有諍訟，若為父母所不開許，是名繫屬於他，不應為授具戒。
items.en: Fifth, being subject to another's authority. A minister of the king; one regarded with hostility by the king; one who has acted against the king; one held captive by a creditor; another's servant or bondsman; one abducted by bandits; one belonging to whoever raised them after separation from their birth parents; one still entangled in unresolved legal dispute; and one whose parents have not given consent — these are called being subject to another's authority, and ordination should not be given.

items.title: Section: A Nāga in Monk's Robes — Why a Shapeshifter Cannot Be Ordained, Even in Genuine Sincerity

items.zh: 若變化者，為護他故，不應為授具戒。所以者何？或有龍等為受法故，自化己身為苾芻像，求受具戒。若便為彼授具戒者，彼睡眠時，便復本形，既睡悟已，作苾芻像，假想苾芻。若守園者、若近事男率爾往趣，見彼身形如是變已，便於一切真苾芻所起憎惡心，謂諸苾芻皆非人類，誰能敬事，施彼衣食。
items.en:
Sixth, protecting others' confidence; first, stating it. Whoever is a shapeshifting being should not, in order to protect others' confidence, be given full ordination. Second, the question raised. Why is this so?
Third, the explanation; first, presenting this category. Certain nāgas and others, wishing to receive the dharma, transform their own body into a monastic's appearance and seek full ordination. Were ordination to be granted, upon falling asleep this being reverts to its true form, and upon waking merely resumes the monastic appearance, only pretending to be a monastic.
Second, explaining the protection of others' confidence. Should a temple caretaker or lay devotee happen upon this transformed form unexpectedly, they would come to feel revulsion towards all genuine monastics, thinking that monastics are not even human at all — who then would revere, serve, or offer them food and clothing?

items.zh: 勿令他人得此惡見，是故為隨護他，不應為彼受具足戒。

blocks.text: A practical passage about who should not receive full ordination, and why. In each case the treatise's concern is the person's freedom and the community's trust.

Damaged motivation, damaged physical basis, damaged male form, damaged wholesome capacity, being bound to another, and protecting others' confidence. The difference that matters is intention: Master Cháng Bǎi, one who presents himself falsely in order to live easily does not gain the vow; one whose motivation turns sincere is different.
Such a person would receive service from teachers and offerings from donors, and both would be very hard to "digest": they would cause wholesome qualities to decline.
The treatise lists three kinds, from birth, intermittent, or by injury. (This rule concerns monks' ordination as the Vinaya defines it.)
Master Cháng Bǎi: nine kinds of people lack self-determination; a king's minister, for instance, needs the king's consent.

The concern is lay devotees' confidence: seeing the true form, they would feel revulsion towards all monastics. (Untranslated, 0592b15: "so that others do not come to this wrong view, one should not give full ordination, to guard them.")
These rules can sound exclusionary to modern ears. The treatise's reasons are practical: a person must be free to choose, able to sustain the life, and not a cause of others losing faith.

quiz.q: What six reasons does the treatise give for not conferring monastic restraint on one who wishes it?
options: being underage, lacking robes and bowl, a teacher's refusal, parents' refusal, too few monks in the assembly, and an improper place
damaged motivation, damaged physical basis, damaged male form, damaged wholesome capacity, being bound to another, protecting others
faithlessness, laziness, forgetfulness, distraction, corrupted wisdom, and bad conduct
killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, intoxicants, and wrong view
quiz.why: The treatise lists damaged motivation, damaged physical basis, damaged male form, damaged wholesome capacity, being bound to another, and protecting others' confidence. Master Cháng Bǎi illustrates the fifth: those without self-determination, such as a person under twenty or someone's servant. Parental refusal is thus one case under the fifth reason, not a reason of its own.

quiz.q: Two people ordain because life at home is hard. When is motivation damaged and when not, according to Master Cháng Bǎi?
options: anyone who ordains because of hardship has damaged motivation and no vow
pretending in order to live easily is damaged and gives no vow; if the mind turns right and one resolves on pure conduct for life, it is not
no one who has gone through the rite has damaged motivation, whatever the motive
coercion by kings or bandits is damaging, but pressure from creditors is not
quiz.why: The hardship is the same in both cases, and the difference is the intention. One who falsely presents himself in order to live easily, Master Cháng Bǎi says, cannot be called ordained and does not gain the vow. One whose motivation turns right, resolving to practise pure conduct for life, cannot be said to have damaged motivation; though the beginning was not pure, this person still gains the monastic vow.

quiz.q: Why should one with a damaged physical basis not ordain?
options: the sick would spread illness through the community, so the rules forbid it
the sick have too heavy a karmic obstruction to practise at all
unable to serve teachers, they would receive service and donors' offerings, both very hard to digest, and their good would decline
the sick have impure motives, seeking only the community's care
quiz.why: The treatise's concern is what follows from being unable to serve: one receives service from teachers and fellow practitioners and offerings from devoted donors, and both kinds are extremely hard to digest and cause wholesome qualities to diminish. Master Cháng Bǎi: such a person can hardly digest these two pure offerings and should not use them. The bar is not a judgement of sincerity.

quiz.q: The English has "being bound in servitude to another," yet the list includes ministers and those without parental consent. What is Master Cháng Bǎi's point?
options: the point is debt: all nine owe money, so the English "bound" is correct
the point is servant status; ministers and the rest are additions by the English
the point is that nine kinds of people lack self-determination; "servitude" narrows it, since ministers and those lacking consent are not enslaved
the point is royal law: all nine are lawbreakers, so it should read "criminal"
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: there are nine kinds of people without self-determination who should not be given full ordination; a king's minister, for instance, must have the king's consent. What they share is not being free to decide for themselves. The English heading "bound in servitude" is narrower than 繫屬, since a minister or a child without parental consent is not a servant.

quiz.q: Why is ordination withheld from nāgas and other shapeshifters? What does "protecting others" protect, per Master Cháng Bǎi?
options: it protects the nāga itself from being harmed by humans
it protects monks from harm by the nāga's powers
it protects beings from criticising and thinking monastics are all transformed spirits
it protects stūpas and temples from destruction by the nāga or defilement by its powers
quiz.why: The harm the treatise fears is to the confidence of caretakers and lay devotees, who on seeing the true form would feel revulsion towards all genuine monastics. Master Cháng Bǎi: it is to protect beings from criticising, thinking monastics are all transformed spirits, and from slandering monks. The nāga's sincerity is not what is at issue.
